newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate leader calls for lower interest rates.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate leader calls for lower interest rates.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, criticizing the power of the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, on Sunday said he believed interest rates should be lower.
Last week's rattling of stock markets worldwide were an indication of Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's strength, Lott told Fox News Sunday in an interview.

"I've always been a little nervous about the Fed, quite frankly ... I sometimes think they focus too much on one side of the equation rather than the broader basket of things. I'm a little nervous about the degree of independence they have, but at the same time I realize that's very important.
"I don't want to bash them," he said, "and overall they've done a pretty good job ... but I think interest rates should be lower, even than what they are."
Stocks and bonds fell sharply on Friday, then recovered some of their losses, after Greenspan warned in a speech on Thursday night about "irrational exuberance" affecting financial markets.
Lott said on Sunday he thought Greenspan "probably would say now 'I wish I'd chosen some other words.'"
Asked about his relations with President Bill Clinton, Lott said the Republican-controlled Congress planned to proceed in a "trust but verify" mode with the White House.

Clinton could move further toward centrist politics in a second term, Lott predicted, since his "more liberal" advisers -- George Stephanopoulos, Harold Ickes and Leon Panetta -- were leaving the White House.

"Now maybe we can see where the president really is," he said. "You gotta be careful not to be charmed by him, but we come from the same neck of the woods," he added. "It'll be harder for him to charm me, maybe."

Lott said he expects the president to lead and he advised him to "take bold stands." If Clinton seeks confrontation, he added, "then we will give him confrontation, but we should begin by lowering the temperature."
"I actually think our agendas will be in sync in many areas," said the Republican leader. "We can take that and then build on it."
Lott said, however, that the administration, which failed two years ago to institute broad health care reform, should not now attempt to put it through Congress "one slice at a time."

He said Clinton had not been "totally forthcoming" on the problems with Medicare and what solutions may be needed. "But I believe he is thinking very seriously about that. He may make a dramatic move, and if he does we will match it and then the American people and the country will be the beneficiaries."
